newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Damage to Argentine wheat could lift world prices.
newsitem.headline: Damage to Argentine wheat could lift world prices.

text.p: Storms that wreaked havoc on 200,000 hectares of Argentina's wheat crop may end up boosting world wheat prices and force East Asian buyers to turn to other suppliers like Canada or Australia, traders said on Wednesday.

Argentina's Food Undersecretary Felix Cirio said on Tuesday that torrential rain and wind in the heart of the country's southern wheat belt last week may have damaged the quality of up to one million tonnes of wheat.
Buyers in the Philippines and Japan have been looking at Argentina as an alternate supplier of wheat as the country was expecting a bumper harvest this year and U.S. prices are high.
"Reports of the crop damage will spur more interest in other alternative markets like Canada and Australia," a senior trader in a European commodity house in Manila told Reuters.
"Or, Philippine firms will have no choice but to bite U.S. wheat even at high prices," he added.
Two Philippine companies recently bought 20,000 tonnes of Argentine wheat in the first such order for the country, which used to buy all its wheat from the United States.
Philippine flour millers said they had also received offers for an additional 70,000 tonnes of wheat from Argentina.
"The crop damage report does not have any effect on the first order," said an official in a local flour mill.
Japan's Food Agency, which said last week it was considering buying Argentine wheat, reacted coolly to the news of the storm damage.
"We're still waiting for the arrival of Argentine wheat samples and we'll determine whether we should buy it after examining its quality," a Food Agency official said.

Japan is one of the world's largest wheat importers. It would be the first time in 22 years that Tokyo would purchase wheat from a source other than the United States in an attempt to diversify its supply sources.
The Food Agency, the grain trading arm of the Agriculture Ministry, is Japan's sole importer of wheat, barley and rice.
Buyers in Taiwan, which buys no Argentine wheat, said if extensive damage to the Argentine crop was confirmed it may boost U.S. prices.
Argentina's Food Undersecretary said his government would not necessarily cut its new 1996/97 wheat production estimate of 14.9 million tonnes.

He said a new estimate to be released later this week would incorporate analysis of satellite photographs for the first time and would also have to take into account better than expected yields from early harvesting.
"We normally do not consider buying Argentine wheat because Taiwan has high quality requirements," Taiwan Flour Mills Association official Lu Wei-chih said.
Taiwan prefers to buy No.1 grade U.S. wheat, Lu added.
"U.S. wheat prices will rise if Argentine wheat has major damage," he said.

Taiwan buyers will not advance their tender schedules and should remain out of the market until mid-January, traders said. South Korean flour millers shrugged off the Argentine news as they do not import wheat from the country, traders said.
"We haven't imported Argentine wheat for flour milling so far," an official with Cheiljedang Corp said.
An official with Daehan Flour Mills Co Ltd also said that the company does not import Argentine wheat, but the firm was worried that crop damage could boost wheat prices in international markets.
South Korean feed millers may be interested in buying Argentine wheat in the future for animal feed, traders said.
Some of the damaged crop could be downgraded to feed wheat.
"Even though we have not yet imported the wheat, there would be some interest if prices were more attractive than Canadian feed wheat," a local trader said.
The trader said Canadian feed wheat was recently quoted at US$135 a tonne FOB in South Korean ports.
South Korean feed wheat buyers are likely to be interested in purchasing at a price under $140 a tonne C&F, he added.
